This is a bad argument. If a credit card lounge is empty all the time, it won't stay open either. The flyers and customers are demanding more lounges as mentioned in the video. A person in the lounge is going to replace a person not in the lounge at the airport, it's literally a commerical preference. I don't really think TGIF being replaced by a C1 lounge is a net loss for everyone involved. If anything, the airlines' lounges are the bigger culprits and I think they're fully aware of this tradeoff. You can have problems with award travel credit cards, but lounges are really not part of that business. It's more an issue with airline loyalty programs.

You know what is a worse tradeoff that deserves a video? CLEAR at venues and airports. Literally, federal tax dollars that goes into TSA resources are shared with private for-profit use. At least you can't really say that about airport lounges in general--they're all just renters. Also, it's not like the traveling public have an alternative to TSA. Anyone can choose to participate or not for any credit card, but not going through the TSA.

That arc, from exclusivity to mass access to overcrowding, makes the ending land harder: the lounges aren't paid for by the $400–$1,000 fees, they're paid for by everyone who swipes a card. Do you think Delta's 3-hour limit and the 18–24 months it says it needs to get on top of overcrowding will actually work, or will the credit card companies just keep adding cardholders faster than the lounges can expand?
